Introduction:-

The Home Credit Default Risk project aims to develop a predictive model that assesses the likelihood of a loan applicant defaulting on repayment. Home Credit, a consumer-finance company, provides loans to clients with limited or no credit history. By accurately predicting default probability, the company can reduce financial risk while maintaining loan accessibility for underbanked populations.

The original dataset contains over 600,000 client records across multiple linked tables (application, credit history, bureau, and payment data). After extensive preprocessing—handling missing values, removing anomalies, and normalizing features—the cleaned training dataset comprises approximately 307,000 clients, each described by demographic, financial, and behavioral attributes. The target variable TARGET indicates whether a client repaid (0) or defaulted (1) on their loan.

This analysis follows the full CRISP-DM process—data understanding, preparation, modeling, and evaluation—with emphasis on predictive modeling. After comprehensive data cleaning and feature engineering, multiple algorithms are compared: • Model 1: Penalized Logistic Regression (glmnet) • Model 2: Decision Tree (CART) • Model 3: Random Forest (ranger) • Model 4: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)

Model performance is evaluated on a stratified 70 / 30 train–validation split using 5-fold cross-validation. Metrics include AUC, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score. The ultimate objective is to identify the model that not only outperforms the majority-class benchmark (~92 % accuracy but no discrimination) but also provides stable, interpretable predictions that can support risk-aware lending decisions.

1 .Code Chunk 1 — Load Required Libraries

This code chunk loads all the R packages required for data exploration, preprocessing, visualization, and modeling. It includes libraries for data manipulation (dplyr, data.table, tidyr), visualization (ggplot2, GGally), data cleaning (janitor, skimr), and machine learning (caret, tidymodels, ranger, xgboost). Loading these libraries at the beginning ensures all necessary functions are available for the entire analysis workflow—from exploratory data analysis (EDA) to model evaluation.

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

2 .Code Chunk 2 — Load and Inspect the Training Dataset

This code chunk imports the main training dataset (application_train.csv) using fread() for fast and efficient loading, then standardizes column names with clean_names(). It provides an initial overview of the dataset through structure, dimensions, and a preview of the first few rows. Basic summary statistics and data types are examined to understand the variable composition and detect any immediate data quality issues before preprocessing.

## ---- load-data ----
# Use fread() for efficiency
app_train <- fread("application_train.csv") |> clean_names()

# Basic structure check
dim(app_train)

3 .Code Chunk 3 — Basic hygiene and anomaly fixes

What this does • Validates core columns exist. Fail fast if not. • Encodes target as a factor for classification. • Replaces the sentinel 365243 in days_employed with NA. This is a documented anomaly. • Creates leak-safe features: age_years from days_birth, emp_years from days_employed. These are standard transforms used in the book’s preprocessing stage.

## ---- clean-basics ----
# prerequisites: app_train from previous chunk, names are snake_case

# 1) assert required columns exist
stopifnot(all(c("sk_id_curr","target","days_birth","days_employed") %in% names(app_train)))

# 2) target to 2-level factor (0 = Repaid, 1 = Default)
app_train <- app_train |>
  dplyr::mutate(target = factor(target, levels = c(0,1)))

# 3) fix known sentinel in days_employed (365243 means "missing")
app_train <- app_train |>
  dplyr::mutate(days_employed = dplyr::na_if(days_employed, 365243))

# 4) safe human-readable derivatives (no leakage)
app_train <- app_train |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    age_years = -days_birth/365.25,
    emp_years = dplyr::if_else(!is.na(days_employed), -days_employed/365.25, NA_real_)
  )

4 .Code Chunk 4 — Missingness scan and prune high-NA columns

What it does • Quantifies missingness per variable. • Drops columns with ≥80% NA to reduce noise and leakage risk. • Preserves sparse but useful scores (ext_source_1, ext_source_3) if they exist.

How to check • head(miss_pct, 25) shows the worst offenders. • length(drop_cols) shows count to be removed. • Final line should return character(0).

## ---- missing-scan ----
library(dplyr)

# percent NA per column
miss_pct <- sapply(app_train, function(x) mean(is.na(x))) |> sort(decreasing = TRUE)

# inspect top 25
head(miss_pct, 25)
##           commonarea_avg          commonarea_mode          commonarea_medi 
##                0.6987230                0.6987230                0.6987230 
##  nonlivingapartments_avg nonlivingapartments_mode nonlivingapartments_medi 
##                0.6943296                0.6943296                0.6943296 
##     livingapartments_avg    livingapartments_mode    livingapartments_medi 
##                0.6835495                0.6835495                0.6835495 
##            floorsmin_avg           floorsmin_mode           floorsmin_medi 
##                0.6784863                0.6784863                0.6784863 
##          years_build_avg         years_build_mode         years_build_medi 
##                0.6649778                0.6649778                0.6649778 
##              own_car_age             landarea_avg            landarea_mode 
##                0.6599081                0.5937674                0.5937674 
##            landarea_medi         basementarea_avg        basementarea_mode 
##                0.5937674                0.5851596                0.5851596 
##        basementarea_medi             ext_source_1        nonlivingarea_avg 
##                0.5851596                0.5638107                0.5517916 
##       nonlivingarea_mode 
##                0.5517916
# drop columns with ≥ 80% NA, except keep key sparse predictors if present
keep_anyway <- intersect(names(app_train), c("ext_source_1","ext_source_3"))
high_na <- names(miss_pct[miss_pct >= 0.80])
drop_cols <- setdiff(high_na, keep_anyway)

length(drop_cols)      # how many to drop
## [1] 0
drop_cols[1:20]        # preview names
##  [1] NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA
app_train <- app_train |> select(-all_of(drop_cols))

# sanity: confirm removed
intersect(names(app_train), drop_cols)  # should be character(0)
## character(0)

5 .Code Chunk 5 — Build the preprocessing recipe

What it does • Excludes sk_id_curr from modeling if present. • Removes zero/near-zero variance columns. • Imputes numerics by median and factors by mode. • Groups rare factor levels into .rare to stabilize. • One-hot encodes factors. • Fixes skew with Yeo–Johnson, then centers and scales numerics. • Drops highly correlated numerics (>|0.90|).

## ---- recipe-prep ----
library(recipes); library(caret)

# target must be factor already (done earlier)
stopifnot(is.factor(app_train$target))

# mark ID so it’s excluded from predictors
has_id <- "sk_id_curr" %in% names(app_train)

rec <- recipe(target ~ ., data = app_train) %>%
  { if (has_id) update_role(., sk_id_curr, new_role = "ID") else . } %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_nzv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.01, other = ".rare") %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot = TRUE) %>%
  step_YeoJohnson(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_center(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_scale(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_corr(all_numeric_predictors(), threshold = 0.90)

rec_prep   <- prep(rec, training = app_train, verbose = TRUE)
## oper 1 step zv [training] 
## oper 2 step nzv [training] 
## oper 3 step impute median [training] 
## oper 4 step impute mode [training] 
## oper 5 step other [training] 
## oper 6 step dummy [training] 
## oper 7 step YeoJohnson [training] 
## oper 8 step center [training] 
## oper 9 step scale [training] 
## oper 10 step corr [training] 
## The retained training set is ~ 297.98 Mb  in memory.
train_clean <- bake(rec_prep, new_data = NULL)
# drop ID column before modeling
train_clean <- dplyr::select(train_clean, -sk_id_curr)

dim(train_clean)
## [1] 307511    127

7 . Code Chunk 6-Sanity check

This code chunk performs a final validation step to confirm data integrity after preprocessing. It checks that no missing values remain in the cleaned dataset across all variables. Ensuring a complete dataset at this stage is critical, as missing values can lead to biased estimates or model training errors in subsequent predictive modeling steps.

8 . Code Chunk 7 Data Partition — 70/30 stratified split

Purpose • Ensures both training and validation sets are randomly sampled yet keep the same proportion of defaulters (~8%) and repaid cases (~92%). • This stratified sampling prevents bias and maintains target distribution consistency.

We split the training dataset into a 70:30 ratio to validate the model’s performance on the training data. After confirming that the model performs satisfactorily, we will retrain it using the entire training dataset and then evaluate its accuracy on the separate test dataset provided by Kaggle.

If output shows approximately 215k rows in training and 92k in validation, with matching class ratios, your split is successful.

Interpretation: • Training set: 215,259 rows. • Validation set: 92,252 rows. • Class proportions (≈ 8.07 % Default / 91.93 % Repaid) are identical across full, train, and validation samples. • Data is balanced correctly for stratified modeling.

## ---- split-70-30 ----
library(caret)

# Convert target to factor (positive = "Default")
train_clean$target <- factor(ifelse(train_clean$target == 1, "Default", "Repaid"),
                             levels = c("Default","Repaid"))

# Create a 70/30 stratified split to preserve class balance
set.seed(123)
idx <- createDataPartition(train_clean$target, p = 0.70, list = FALSE)

trn <- train_clean[idx, ]   # training subset (70%)
val <- train_clean[-idx, ]  # validation subset (30%)

# Check structure and class proportions
dim(trn); dim(val)
## [1] 215259    127
## [1] 92252   127
prop.table(table(train_clean$target))
## 
##    Default     Repaid 
## 0.08072882 0.91927118
prop.table(table(trn$target))
## 
##    Default     Repaid 
## 0.08073065 0.91926935
prop.table(table(val$target))
## 
##    Default     Repaid 
## 0.08072454 0.91927546

9 . Code CHunk -8 Benchmark majority classifier

Computes the majority-class baseline. Predicts all as “Repaid,” then reports Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, and AUC=0.5. Establishes the must-beat benchmark.

## ---- benchmark-majority ----
# Always predict "Repaid" on validation
bench_pred <- factor(rep("Repaid", nrow(val)), levels = c("Default","Repaid"))
bench_cm   <- caret::confusionMatrix(bench_pred, val$target, positive = "Default")

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Metric = c("Accuracy","Precision","Recall","Specificity","F1","AUC"),
  Value  = c(
    bench_cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    bench_cm$byClass["Precision"],
    bench_cm$byClass["Sensitivity"],
    bench_cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    bench_cm$byClass["F1"],
    0.5  # random ranking baseline
  )
), digits = 4, caption = "Benchmark — Majority Class (predict all Repaid)")

9.1 . metrics-helper

Defines reusable evaluators. Given predicted probabilities and truth, it computes ROC/AUC, confusion matrices at 0.50 and Youden thresholds, and formats metric tables.

## ---- metrics-helper ----
library(pROC); library(caret); library(knitr)
## Type 'citation("pROC")' for a citation.
## 
## Attaching package: 'pROC'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
## 
##     cov, smooth, var
eval_probs <- function(p, truth, thresh = 0.50) {
  roc_obj <- roc(truth, p, levels = c("Repaid","Default"))
  auc_val <- as.numeric(auc(roc_obj))
  # fixed threshold
  yhat <- factor(ifelse(p >= thresh, "Default","Repaid"), levels = c("Default","Repaid"))
  cm   <- confusionMatrix(yhat, truth, positive = "Default")
  # Youden threshold
  t_opt <- as.numeric(coords(roc_obj, "best", best.method = "youden", ret = "threshold"))
  yopt  <- factor(ifelse(p >= t_opt, "Default","Repaid"), levels = c("Default","Repaid"))
  cm2   <- confusionMatrix(yopt, truth, positive = "Default")

  list(
    auc = auc_val, t_opt = t_opt, roc = roc_obj,
    fixed = cm, optimal = cm2
  )
}

print_metrics <- function(tag, res) {
  kable(data.frame(
    Metric = c("AUC","Threshold","Accuracy","Precision","Recall","Specificity","F1"),
    `@0.50` = c(
      sprintf("%.4f", res$auc),
      "0.50",
      sprintf("%.4f", res$fixed$overall["Accuracy"]),
      sprintf("%.4f", res$fixed$byClass["Precision"]),
      sprintf("%.4f", res$fixed$byClass["Sensitivity"]),
      sprintf("%.4f", res$fixed$byClass["Specificity"]),
      sprintf("%.4f", res$fixed$byClass["F1"])
    ),
    `@Youden` = c(
      sprintf("%.4f", res$auc),
      sprintf("%.3f", res$t_opt),
      sprintf("%.4f", res$optimal$overall["Accuracy"]),
      sprintf("%.4f", res$optimal$byClass["Precision"]),
      sprintf("%.4f", res$optimal$byClass["Sensitivity"]),
      sprintf("%.4f", res$optimal$byClass["Specificity"]),
      sprintf("%.4f", res$optimal$byClass["F1"])
    )
  ), align = "lcc", caption = paste(tag, "— Metrics Summary"))
}

10 . Model 1 — Penalized Logistic Regression (glmnet)

Purpose • Fits a regularized logistic regression using both L1 (lasso) and L2 (ridge) penalties. • Performs internal 5-fold CV to pick the best penalty strength (lambda) and mixing parameter (alpha) that maximize AUC. • Provides interpretable coefficients and a strong baseline.

## ---- model1-glmnet-train ----
library(caret)
library(glmnet)
## Loading required package: Matrix
## 
## Attaching package: 'Matrix'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:tidyr':
## 
##     expand, pack, unpack
## Loaded glmnet 4.1-10
# Cross-validation setup
ctrl <- trainControl(
  method = "cv", number = 5,              # 5-fold CV
  classProbs = TRUE,                      # compute probabilities
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,      # use ROC metric
  savePredictions = "final"
)

# Train penalized logistic regression (elastic-net)
set.seed(123)
m_glmnet <- caret::train(
  target ~ ., data = trn,
  method = "glmnet",
  trControl = ctrl,
  metric = "ROC",                         # maximize AUC
  tuneLength = 10                         # search grid of alpha / lambda
)

# View cross-validation results

10.1 . Code Chunk — Validate Model

Purpose • Tests the model on unseen validation data. • Calculates ROC AUC, the main metric for credit-risk models. • Plots ROC curve to visualize discrimination ability.

output:-

Model 1 — Penalized Logistic Regression (glmnet) Performance Summary

Metric Value Interpretation
Validation AUC ≈ 0.739 Moderate–strong discrimination. In credit-risk modeling, any AUC between 0.70–0.80 is considered a good baseline.
Cross-validated AUC ≈ 0.742 Consistent with validation. Indicates stable performance and minimal overfitting.
Sensitivity / Specificity ≈ 0.004 / 0.999 Default cases rare. Low recall due to imbalance, which is normal before re-weighting or re-sampling. 
•   Logistic (even penalized) models capture linear effects only.
•   The dataset has nonlinear, interaction-heavy patterns (age × income × credit etc.).
•   Tree-based and boosting models (next steps) usually raise AUC to 0.77–0.82 on this data.

So: • glmnet is solid as a baseline — interpretable and well-behaved. • Expect stronger performance from Random Forest and Gradient Boosting.

## ---- model1-glmnet-validate ----
library(pROC)

# Predict default probabilities on validation data
pred_val <- predict(m_glmnet, newdata = val, type = "prob")[, "Default"]

# Compute ROC and AUC
roc_obj <- roc(response = val$target, predictor = pred_val, levels = c("Repaid","Default"))
## Setting direction: controls < cases
auc(roc_obj)
## Area under the curve: 0.739
plot(roc_obj, col = "steelblue", main = "ROC Curve — Model 1: Penalized Logistic Regression")

Applies the evaluator to glmnet predictions. Prints confusion matrices and metric tables at 0.50 and Youden. Confirms threshold-dependent trade-offs.

res1 <- eval_probs(pred_val, val$target, thresh = 0.50)
## Setting direction: controls < cases
print_metrics("Model 1: Penalized Logistic (glmnet)", res1)

11 . Model 2 — Decision Tree (CART)

A single CART tree shows how features split borrowers into default vs repaid groups. This model is simple, interpretable, and forms the foundation for ensembles (Bagging, RF, GBM).

##. Code Chunk — Train CART Model

Purpose • Fits a CART model using Gini-based recursive partitioning. • Performs 5-fold CV to find the optimal complexity parameter cp. • Gives an interpretable tree with primary splits like EXT_SOURCE_2, DAYS_BIRTH, etc.

## ---- model2-cart-train ----
library(caret)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)

# 1. Cross-validation setup
ctrl_cart <- trainControl(
  method = "cv", number = 5,
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
  savePredictions = "final"
)

# 2. Train classification tree
set.seed(123)
m_cart <- caret::train(
  target ~ ., data = trn,
  method = "rpart",
  trControl = ctrl_cart,
  metric = "ROC",          # maximize AUC
  tuneLength = 10
)

# 3. View model summary and plot complexity parameter (cp)
m_cart

12 .Model 3 — Random Forest (ranger)

12.1 .Code Chunk — Train Random Forest

Trains a weighted Random Forest with 5-fold cross-validation. Tunes mtry and min.node.size. Uses class weights to address imbalance. Evaluates on the validation set and reports ROC AUC. Outputs a concise summary table for inclusion in the report.

## ---- model3-rf-train ----
library(caret)
library(ranger)

# 1) CV setup
ctrl_rf <- trainControl(
  method = "cv", number = 5,
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
  savePredictions = "final"
)

# 2) Class weights (inverse frequency)
tbl <- table(trn$target)
w_default <- as.numeric(tbl["Repaid"])  / sum(tbl)  # weight minority higher
w_repaid  <- as.numeric(tbl["Default"]) / sum(tbl)
class_wts <- c("Default" = w_default, "Repaid" = w_repaid)

# 3) Tune grid
p <- ncol(trn) - 1
tgrid <- expand.grid(
  mtry = unique(pmax(1, round(c(sqrt(p)/2, sqrt(p), 2*sqrt(p))))),
  splitrule = "gini",
  min.node.size = c(5, 20)
)

# 4) Train
set.seed(123)
m_rf <- caret::train(
  target ~ ., data = trn,
  method = "ranger",
  trControl = ctrl_rf,
  metric = "ROC",
  tuneGrid = tgrid,
  importance = "impurity",
  num.trees = 500,
  class.weights = class_wts
)

13 . Model 4 — Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)

13.1 . Code Chunk — Train XGBoost

Fits a weighted XGBoost classifier with 5-fold CV. Tunes depth, learning rate, rounds, gamma, and child weight. Handles class imbalance via sample weights. Evaluates on the validation set with ROC AUC.

## ---- model4-xgb-train ----
library(caret); library(xgboost); library(doParallel)
## 
## Attaching package: 'xgboost'
## The following object is masked from 'package:dplyr':
## 
##     slice
## Loading required package: foreach
## 
## Attaching package: 'foreach'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:purrr':
## 
##     accumulate, when
## Loading required package: iterators
## Loading required package: parallel
# parallel
cl <- makeCluster(parallel::detectCores() - 1); registerDoParallel(cl)

# class weights (inverse frequency)
tbl <- table(trn$target)
w_map <- c("Default" = as.numeric(tbl["Repaid"])/sum(tbl),
          "Repaid"  = as.numeric(tbl["Default"])/sum(tbl))
trn_wts <- w_map[trn$target]

# CV setup
ctrl_xgb <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5,
                         classProbs = TRUE,
                         summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
                         savePredictions = "final")

# modest tuning grid
tgrid <- expand.grid(
  nrounds = c(200, 400),
  max_depth = c(3, 6),
  eta = c(0.05, 0.10),
  gamma = c(0, 1),
  colsample_bytree = c(0.7),
  min_child_weight = c(1, 5),
  subsample = c(0.8)
)

set.seed(123)
m_xgb <- caret::train(
  target ~ ., data = trn,
  method = "xgbTree",
  trControl = ctrl_xgb,
  metric = "ROC",
  tuneGrid = tgrid,
  weights = trn_wts,
  verbose = FALSE
)

stopCluster(cl); registerDoSEQ()

m_xgb

  1. Experiment Proposal

Objective

The purpose of this experiment is to design, train, and evaluate multiple machine learning models to predict the probability that a loan applicant will default on repayment. By comparing several modeling approaches and evaluation metrics, the goal is to identify the most accurate and reliable model for credit risk assessment in the Home Credit Default Risk dataset.

Research Question

Can advanced machine learning models such as Random Forest and Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) outperform baseline statistical models (e.g., Logistic Regression) in predicting loan defaults, while maintaining interpretability and robustness?

Experimental Design

1.  *Dataset and Inputs*

•   Source: Home Credit Default Risk dataset (application_train.csv).
•   Total observations (after cleaning): ~307,000 clients.
•   Target variable: TARGET — binary (0 = Repaid, 1 = Default).
•   Predictors: Financial, demographic, and credit history features derived from applicant data.

2.  *Data Preparation*

•   Cleaned and normalized features using recipes pipeline.
•   Removed high-NA and zero-variance predictors.
•   Handled imbalance via class weights (and later threshold-based evaluation).
•   Derived engineered variables such as AGE_YEARS, EMP_YEARS, and log-scaled financial ratios.

3.  *Experimental Methodology*

•   Partitioning: 70% training / 30% validation, stratified by target variable.
•   Cross-Validation: 5-fold CV for parameter tuning and model stability.
•   Benchmark: Majority-class classifier predicting all as “Repaid” (Accuracy ≈ 0.919, AUC = 0.5).
•   Models Tested:
•   Model 1 — Penalized Logistic Regression (glmnet)
•   Model 2 — Decision Tree (CART)
•   Model 3 — Random Forest (ranger)
•   Model 4 — Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)

4.  *Evaluation Metrics*

•   Primary metric: AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve).
•   Secondary metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Specificity, and F1 Score.
•   Diagnostics: Confusion matrices at fixed (0.50) and optimal (Youden) thresholds.
•   Performance Goal: Achieve AUC > 0.70 and improved recall over the baseline model.

5.  *Expected Outcomes*

•   Determine the model with the best discrimination between repaid and defaulted loans.
•   Quantify trade-offs between precision and recall for credit risk decisions.
•   Validate that boosting methods (especially XGBoost) deliver the best overall balance between predictive power and generalization.

Significance

Accurately predicting default risk will help Home Credit improve lending decisions, reduce financial losses, and extend fair credit access to low-history borrowers. The experiment also provides practical experience in end-to-end machine learning model development, imbalanced classification, and performance evaluation using real-world financial data.
